newsitem.title: UK: Brit Biotech to seek drug approval Q1 1997.
newsitem.headline: Brit Biotech to seek drug approval Q1 1997.

text.p: British Biotech Plc said on Wednesday that Phase III trials on its acute pancreatitis drug Lexipafant were "positive" and that its plan to apply for European marketing approval for the drug in the first quarter of 1997 was on track.
In a statement British Biotech said Lexipafant, which is its lead product in terms of timing, would be marketed under the name Zacutex.
The company also announced a second-quarter loss of 8.1 million stg, bringing the loss for the first half to 16.1 million stg. The second half loss was broadly in line with analysts' expectations.

British Biotech said European Phase III trials of Lexipafant on 290 patients showed "a clear treatment effect, with an improvement in organ failure scores in patients treated with Zacutex against placebo and fewer deaths in the Zacutex-treated group of patients."
Acute pancreatitis, which principally attacks the liver and kidneys and causes death in around 10 percent of patients, is currently a poorly treated disease.
The company said marketing plans for the drug are well advanced. It plans to market the drug itself in Europe and North America.
However, there will be more concern over the group's stem cell protector drug BB-10010, which is being developed to ease side-effects linked to chemotherapy and as a possible HIV treatment.

The company said initial results from the first of five Phase II, or intermediate, trials designed to examine the drug's ability to protect bone marrow from damage during chemotherapy "are not encouraging."
The company also said it intended to drop development of anti-cancer agent, Batimastat.

In a statement the company said the injectable drug, which was its lead project at one stage, had a similar profile to the oral anti-cancer treatment Marimastat, which has now entered late stage clinical trials.
Analysts said the news on Batimastat, which was the group's lead product at one stage, had been well-flagged.

"Given the ease of Marimastat's administration by mouth, the success of Phase II trials in late-stage cancer patients and the commencement of Marimastat Phase III trials in lung cancer and shortly ovarian cancer, British Biotech has decided to discontinue development of Batimastat as an anti-cancer agent," the company said.
The statement coincided with the announcemnt of second-quarter results and detail of late-stage trials on its lead product, acute pancreatitis treatment Lexipafant.
